messages.content: How do you say "The meeting has been moved to Friday because the manager is traveling" in Spanish?

«La reunión se ha trasladado al viernes porque el gerente está de viaje.»

Two things worth noticing: Spanish uses the present perfect «se ha trasladado» here because the change still matters now, and «estar de viaje» is the fixed expression for being away traveling — you don't say «está viajando» in this context.
¿Qué planes tienes para este fin de semana?

El sábado por la mañana quiero ir al mercado a comprar verduras frescas, y por la tarde voy a visitar a mi hermana. El domingo prefiero descansar en casa y leer un poco. ¿Y tú? ¿Vas a hacer algo especial?
Yo voy a la playa con unos amigos si hace buen tiempo.
¡Qué bien! Si hace sol, no olvides la crema solar. La última vez que fui a la playa volví rojo como un tomate.
¿Cuál es la diferencia entre «ser» y «estar»? Siempre los confundo.

La regla clásica ayuda: «ser» describe lo que algo ES por naturaleza — origen, profesión, características permanentes. «Estar» describe cómo está algo en un momento — estado, ubicación, emociones.

Ejemplos:
- «Soy médico» (profesión, ser).
- «Estoy cansado» (estado temporal, estar).
- «La sopa es fría» sería raro; lo normal es «la sopa está fría», porque es su estado ahora.

Ojo con los adjetivos que cambian de significado: «ser aburrido» = ser una persona aburrida; «estar aburrido» = sentirse aburrido ahora. Y «ser listo» = ser inteligente, pero «estar listo» = estar preparado.
Can you correct my Spanish? "Yo soy hambre y la casa es cerca del parque."

Two classic traps in one sentence. Corrected: «Tengo hambre y la casa está cerca del parque.»

1. Hunger in Spanish is something you HAVE, not something you are: «tener hambre» (also «tener sed», «tener frío», «tener sueño»).
2. Location always takes «estar», even for a house that never moves: «la casa está cerca del parque». «Ser» is for where an event takes place, not where a thing is.
Translate this into English: «No te preocupes, ya casi llegamos; el tráfico está pesado, pero el conductor conoce un atajo.»

"Don't worry, we're almost there; traffic is heavy, but the driver knows a shortcut."

«Ya casi llegamos» is literally "we're already almost arriving" — Spanish states the near-future as nearly done. And «está pesado» for traffic is idiomatic; a word-for-word «heavy» works in English here by luck, not by rule.
¿Qué significa «estar en las nubes»?

Significa estar distraído, con la mente en otra parte, sin prestar atención a lo que pasa a tu alrededor.

Ejemplo: «Durante la reunión, Juan estaba en las nubes y no escuchó la pregunta del jefe.»

El equivalente en inglés sería "to have your head in the clouds" — una de las pocas veces en que la imagen coincide casi exactamente en los dos idiomas.
Buenas tardes, ¿tienen una mesa para dos?
Buenas tardes, bienvenidos. Sí, tenemos una mesa junto a la ventana. ¿Les traigo algo de beber mientras miran la carta?
Para mí, un agua con gas. Y de primero quiero la sopa del día.
Perfecto. ¿Y para acompañar? ¿Ha visto ya el plato principal o le recomiendo el pescado de hoy?
Why is it "cuando llegue a casa" and not "cuando llega a casa"? Isn't it present tense?

Because after «cuando», Spanish splits by time reference. For habits and present facts, the indicative works: «Cuando llego a casa, ceno» (every day, when I get home, I eat dinner). But for a single FUTURE event, Spanish requires the subjunctive: «Cuando llegue a casa, te llamo» — the arrival hasn't happened yet, so it isn't presented as a fact.

Same pattern with «en cuanto», «hasta que», «antes de que»: «En cuanto termine la clase, salimos.» English hides this completely ("when I get home" covers both), which is why it trips up English speakers.
I need a polite way to open a formal email in Spanish: "Dear Mr. Herrera, I am writing to ask about the status of my application."

«Estimado señor Herrera:

Le escribo para consultarle sobre el estado de mi solicitud.»

Notes: «Estimado» is the standard formal opener (never translate "dear" as «querido» in business writing — that's affectionate). Spanish formal letters use a colon after the greeting, not a comma. And «le escribo» with the indirect-object «le» keeps the tone courteous and distant, which is exactly right here.
Por vs para — give me a way to finally keep them straight.

Think of «para» as an arrow pointing FORWARD to a goal, and «por» as a path going THROUGH or an exchange.

PARA (destination/purpose/deadline):
- «Este regalo es para ti» (recipient)
- «Salimos para Madrid» (destination)
- «Lo necesito para el lunes» (deadline)
- «Estudia para aprobar» (purpose)

POR (through/exchange/cause/duration):
- «Caminamos por el parque» (through)
- «Te doy las gracias por tu ayuda» (in exchange/because of)
- «Lo compré por veinte euros» (price)
- «Trabajó por tres horas» (duration)

The famous contrast: «Lo hice por ti» = I did it because of you / on your behalf. «Lo hice para ti» = I did it for you to have. Same words, different story.
Perdone, ¿sabe dónde queda la estación de tren?
Sí, claro. Siga todo recto por esta calle unos cinco minutos y gire a la izquierda en el segundo semáforo. La estación está justo enfrente de la plaza, no tiene pérdida.
¿Y queda muy lejos a pie?
No, unos diez minutos andando. Si prefiere, también puede tomar el autobús número 4 aquí mismo, en esta parada, y bajar en la tercera parada.
How would you translate the saying «Más vale tarde que nunca» and is it used the same way as in English?

"Better late than never" — and yes, it's used in almost exactly the same situations: someone arrives late, a payment shows up after the deadline, a reply comes weeks later.

Spanish is rich in these «más vale» proverbs. A close cousin is «Más vale prevenir que curar» — "better safe than sorry," literally "better to prevent than to cure." Both languages reach for the same consolation; Spanish just has a whole family of them built on the same frame.
Correct this please: "Me gusto mucho la película de anoche."

Corrected: «Me gustó mucho la película de anoche.»

Two fixes hiding in one word. First, the accent: «gustó» (past, he/she/it pleased) vs «gusto» (present, I please). Second — and this is the deeper point — «gustar» works backwards from English. The movie is the subject: the sentence really says "the movie pleased me a lot." That's why it's «me gustó la película» (singular movie) but «me gustaron las películas» (plural). You're not the one doing the liking grammatically; the thing liked controls the verb.
My Spanish friend said "¡Me estás tomando el pelo!" when I told her I won the lottery (I hadn't). What did she mean?

She meant "You're pulling my leg!" — «tomar el pelo» is literally "to take someone's hair," and it's the standard way to say someone is teasing or joking with you.

A natural reply once the joke lands: «¡Es broma!» (it's a joke). Careful with the false friend: «tomar el pelo» has nothing to do with haircuts. Spanish also says «quedarse con alguien» in Spain for the same idea — to mess with someone.
Doctor, me duele la garganta desde el lunes y tengo un poco de fiebre.
Entiendo. ¿La fiebre es alta? ¿Ha tomado algo para bajarla?
Solo paracetamol. También me duelen los oídos cuando trago.
Voy a examinarle la garganta. Es posible que sea una infección; si es bacteriana, le recetaré un antibiótico. Beba muchos líquidos y descanse. Si la fiebre no baja en dos días, vuelva a verme.
¿Cuándo uso el pretérito y cuándo el imperfecto? Entiendo las formas, pero no la elección.

Piensa en una película. El pretérito es la cámara que AVANZA la historia: eventos completos, uno tras otro. El imperfecto es el ESCENARIO: el fondo, lo que estaba pasando mientras tanto.

«Ayer salí de casa (pretérito), caminé al mercado (pretérito) y compré pan (pretérito).» — tres eventos en cadena.

«Hacía sol y la gente paseaba (imperfecto) cuando de repente empezó a llover (pretérito).» — el imperfecto pinta el fondo; el pretérito irrumpe.

Regla práctica: si puedes preguntar «¿y luego qué pasó?», va pretérito. Si la frase responde «¿cómo era todo en ese momento?», va imperfecto.
Translate into Spanish: "If I had known about the traffic, I would have left an hour earlier."

«Si hubiera sabido lo del tráfico, habría salido una hora antes.»

This is the classic unreal past conditional, and Spanish needs the subjunctive in both halves' machinery: «si hubiera sabido» (pluperfect subjunctive after «si» for an impossible past) plus «habría salido» (conditional perfect). One common slip: never put the conditional in the «si» clause — «si habría sabido» is wrong. You may also hear «si hubiese sabido»; the -se form is equally correct, just slightly more literary.
¡Feliz cumpleaños, Marta! ¿Cuántos cumples?
¡Muchas gracias! Cumplo treinta y dos, aunque no los aparento, ¿verdad?
¡Para nada! Te conservas muy bien. ¿Dónde vas a celebrarlo?
En casa de mis padres, con una cena pequeña. Mi madre va a preparar mi plato favorito y habrá pastel de chocolate, como debe ser.
Where do the little words go in "I want to give it to her" — le lo, se lo? I'm confused.

The finished sentence: «Quiero dárselo» or «Se lo quiero dar.»

Step by step: "it" = «lo», "to her" = «le». But Spanish forbids «le lo» side by side — when both pronouns start with L, the first one changes to «se»: «se lo». It looks like a reflexive but it isn't; it's a repair rule.

Placement: with an infinitive, pronouns attach to the end («dárselo», note the accent to keep the stress) or ride in front of the conjugated verb («se lo quiero dar»). Both are equally correct.
¿Qué es la sobremesa? Mi familia española se queda en la mesa muchísimo tiempo después de comer.

Has descubierto una institución. La sobremesa es el tiempo que se pasa conversando en la mesa después de terminar de comer, sin prisa, a veces una hora o más. No es un postre ni una actividad: es la conversación misma.

Es tan central que en España y América Latina levantarse de la mesa justo después del último bocado puede parecer casi brusco. El café, un licor, las historias de siempre... todo eso ES la comida, socialmente hablando. Si te quedas y participas, ya eres de la familia.
Translate this news sentence into English: «El ayuntamiento anunció que el nuevo parque abrirá sus puertas la próxima primavera, tras dos años de obras.»

"The city council announced that the new park will open its doors next spring, after two years of construction work."

Two translator's choices: «ayuntamiento» is the municipal government — "city hall" works too, but "city council" fits the announcement context. And «abrirá sus puertas» is the standard formula for a venue opening; English happens to share the image ("open its doors"), so keep it rather than flattening it to just "will open."
Is "Ayer he ido al mercado" wrong? I learned present perfect for recent past.

It's not wrong everywhere — but it will sound off in most of Latin America. In much of Spain, «ayer he ido» is perfectly normal for a past event in a time period that feels connected to today. In Mexico, Argentina, Colombia and most of Latin America, the preterite rules: «Ayer fui al mercado.»

Practical advice: learn the preterite for finished past events («fui», «compré», «llegué») as your default, and reserve «he ido» for experiences without a stated time («¿Has estado en Perú?»). You'll be understood everywhere.
Hola, llamo para pedir una cita para cortarme el pelo, por favor.
Hola, con gusto. ¿Tiene preferencia por algún día? Tenemos espacio este jueves por la tarde o el sábado por la mañana.
El sábado por la mañana me viene mejor. ¿A qué hora sería?
Tenemos a las diez o a las once y media. La dejo anotada para el sábado a las diez, ¿le parece? Solo necesito su nombre y un teléfono de contacto.
Why does Spanish say "se me cayó el vaso" instead of just "yo dejé caer el vaso"? Who is "se" here?

This is the famous accidental «se» — and it's a kindness built into the grammar. «Se me cayó el vaso» frames the event as something that HAPPENED to you, not something you did: literally "the glass fell itself from me."

The pattern: se + indirect pronoun (me/te/le) + verb agreeing with the THING. «Se me olvidaron las llaves» (the keys forgot themselves on me — note the plural verb for «llaves»). «Se le rompió el coche.» Compare «Yo rompí el vaso», which openly admits you broke it. Spanish speakers reach for the «se» version constantly, because life, grammatically, is something that happens to us.
How do I say "She had already left when we arrived" in Spanish?

«Ella ya se había ido cuando llegamos.»

The tense doing the work is the pluperfect: «había ido» — "had left" — for the event that finished BEFORE another past event. The timeline: her leaving (earlier, pluperfect) → our arrival (later, simple preterite «llegamos»). Spanish also needs the reflexive here: leaving a place is «irse», not «ir», so «se había ido». Without the «se» you'd be saying she had gone somewhere, not that she had left.
How do you say "I'm looking forward to seeing you next week" in Portuguese?

«Estou ansioso por te ver na próxima semana» — or, more neutral and very common: «Mal posso esperar para te ver na próxima semana» ("I can hardly wait to see you").

A warning about the literal trap: «olhar para a frente» would be nonsense here. English "look forward to" is an idiom, so Portuguese answers with its own idioms. In Brazilian Portuguese you'd also hear «Estou contando os dias para te ver» — counting the days.
Bom dia! Um café, por favor. Tem pastel de nata hoje?
Bom dia! Temos, sim, saíram do forno há pouco. Quer o pastel quentinho, com canela e açúcar?
Quero, sim. E o café bem forte, por favor.
Perfeito. Um café forte e um pastel de nata quentinho. Mais alguma coisa? Temos sumo de laranja natural, espremido agora mesmo.
O que é «saudade»? Já ouvi dizer que não tem tradução.

É verdade que não existe uma palavra igual nas outras línguas, mas o sentimento é universal. «Saudade» é a presença de uma ausência: a dor boa de sentir falta de alguém, de um lugar ou de um tempo que já passou — e que talvez não volte.

Repara que se pode ter saudade de algo que nunca se viveu: «Tenho saudade do que não vivi.» Em inglês, o mais próximo é uma frase inteira: "a deep longing for something gone." A palavra é tão central que o português a usa no plural, «saudades», quando a emoção é grande: «Tenho tantas saudades tuas.»
Correct my Portuguese: "Eu sou com fome e vou comer agora."

Corrected: «Estou com fome e vou comer agora.»

Hunger in Portuguese is a temporary state, so it takes «estar», not «ser» — the same logic as Spanish. And the fixed pattern is «estar com fome» (to be WITH hunger). The family: «estar com sede» (thirsty), «estar com sono» (sleepy), «estar com pressa» (in a hurry). Your verb «vou comer» was already perfect — the future with «ir» + infinitive is exactly how Brazilians and Portuguese say it daily.
Translate into English: «Apesar da chuva, a festa continuou até de madrugada, e ninguém quis ir embora.»

"Despite the rain, the party went on until the early hours of the morning, and nobody wanted to leave."

«Apesar de» is the workhorse for "despite/in spite of" — followed by a noun here, or by an infinitive: «apesar de chover». And «de madrugada» is a chunk worth memorizing: Portuguese treats the small hours as a time-block, so "until dawn-ish" is one fixed expression, not a preposition puzzle.
What does "ficar de olho" mean? A colleague told me to "ficar de olho no prazo."

It means "to keep an eye on" — literally "to stay with an eye on." Your colleague was telling you to watch the deadline closely.

The verb «ficar» is doing heavy lifting: it means stay/become/remain, and it anchors dozens of expressions. «Ficar de olho em algo» (keep an eye on something), «ficar sabendo» (to find out), «ficar à vontade» (make yourself comfortable). This is one case where English and Portuguese share the exact same image, so it's an easy one to keep.
When do I use «tu» and when «você»? My textbook uses both and I'm lost.

Geography decides. In most of Brazil, «você» is the everyday "you" for almost everyone — friends, colleagues, strangers — and «tu» survives mainly in the south and parts of the north, often mixed with «você» verb forms. In Portugal it's the opposite: «tu» is the normal informal you, and «você» can sound stiff or even rude; the Portuguese often drop the pronoun entirely or use «o senhor / a senhora» for politeness.

Practical rule: Brazil → «você» everywhere, verbs in third person («você quer?»). Portugal → «tu» with friends («tu queres?»), and for formal situations, name the person: «O senhor deseja?»
Que dia lindo! Vamos à praia amanhã?
Vamos! A previsão diz que vai fazer sol o dia todo. Saímos cedo para arranjar um bom lugar na areia?
Boa ideia. Eu levo a sombrinha e as cadeiras.
E eu levo a caixa térmica com água e fruta. Encontramo-nos às nove em frente à tua casa, então. Não te esqueças do protetor solar desta vez!
Translate into Portuguese: "If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home and watch a film."

«Se chover amanhã, ficamos em casa e vemos um filme.»

The interesting part is «se chover»: after «se" (if) referring to the future, Portuguese uses the future subjunctive — a tense Spanish lost. «Chover» is irregular here: chover → chover (it happens to match the infinitive for regular -er verbs in this tense, but for «ir» it becomes «se eu for»). The main clause can be present («ficamos») or «vamos ficar»; both are natural.
My grammar book mentions the "personal infinitive" in Portuguese. What is it and when do I need it?

Portuguese has something no other major Romance language kept: an infinitive that conjugates. «Falar» becomes «eu falar, tu falares, ele falar, nós falarmos, eles falarem» — the infinitive wearing person endings.

You need it when an infinitive has its own subject, different from the main verb's: «É importante eles chegarem cedo» (it's important FOR THEM to arrive early — «chegarem» marks the "them"). Also after prepositions with a specific subject: «Antes de sairmos, apaga a luz» (before WE leave). If the subject is the same as the main clause, plain infinitive suffices: «Quero sair.»
Correct this: "Nós vai à praia amanhã porque o tempo está bom."

Almost — just the verb agreement: «Nós vamos à praia amanhã porque o tempo está bom.»

«Nós» always takes the -mos form: vamos, estamos, queremos, falamos. Your «à praia» was correct, by the way: «ir» + «a» + «a praia» contracts into that accented «à» (the crase). It's one of the most-missed accents in written Portuguese, and you got it right.
A Brazilian friend said she ended up "pagando o pato" at work. Paying the duck??

She took the blame for something that wasn't her fault — or paid for others' mistakes. «Pagar o pato» = to be the one who ends up holding the bill, literally and figuratively, for a mess you didn't make.

Example: «O erro foi da equipa toda, mas quem pagou o pato fui eu.» (The whole team made the mistake, but I was the one who paid for it.) The duck's origin is disputed — likely from an old market trick — but the meaning is universal: every office knows who ends up paying the duck.
Quanto custa este lenço de seda?
Esse custa quarenta euros, senhora. É seda verdadeira, feita à mão.
É bonito, mas está um pouco caro para mim. Faz-me um desconto?
Posso fazer-lhe trinta e cinco, por ser o último que temos nesta cor. Fica-lhe muito bem, combina com os seus olhos.
Translate into English: «Quem espera sempre alcança, mas quem não se mexe fica a ver navios.»

"Whoever waits always achieves — but whoever doesn't move is left watching the ships go by."

This stitches two Portuguese sayings together. «Quem espera sempre alcança» is the patient person's motto (roughly "good things come to those who wait"). The second half is the corrective: «ficar a ver navios» — "to be left watching ships" — means to be left empty-handed, waiting for something that never arrives. Legend ties it to Lisbon crowds watching for a king's ship that never returned. Together: patience works, but only if you also move.
Why is it "no parque" and "na praia"? Where did the "em" go?

It didn't disappear — it fused. Portuguese contracts «em» (in/on/at) with the article: em + o = «no», em + a = «na», em + os = «nos», em + as = «nas». So «no parque» = in the park, «na praia» = at the beach.

These contractions are not optional decoration; «em o parque» is simply wrong. The same fusion happens with «de»: de + o = «do» («o carro do João»), and with «a»: a + a = «à». Learn the four «em» forms as single words and your Portuguese instantly sounds twice as natural.
How do you say "Could you please repeat that more slowly? I didn't understand the last part" in French?

« Pourriez-vous répéter plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ? Je n'ai pas compris la dernière partie. »

« Pourriez-vous » is the conditional of « pouvoir » — the polite-request form, much softer than « pouvez-vous ». Notice French typography: a space goes before the question mark. And « la dernière partie » for "the last part" — « partie » is the word for a part of a whole, while « part » alone means a share.
Bonjour ! Je voudrais une baguette et deux croissants, s'il vous plaît.
Bonjour ! Bien sûr. La baguette, vous la voulez bien cuite ou pas trop ?
Bien cuite, merci. Et un pain au chocolat pour mon fils.
Voilà : une baguette bien cuite, deux croissants et un pain au chocolat. Ça fera six euros vingt, s'il vous plaît.
Passé composé or imparfait? I know both forms but never know which one a sentence wants.

Ask what the sentence is DOING. The passé composé reports events with edges — they start, finish, move the story: « Hier, j'ai pris le train et je suis arrivé à huit heures. » The imparfait paints everything without edges — weather, feelings, habits, background: « Il faisait beau, les gens se promenaient. »

The classic combined pattern: « Je marchais dans la rue (imparfait, ongoing) quand j'ai vu Marie (passé composé, interruption). »

Quick test: if you can count it ("three times", "once", "suddenly"), it's passé composé. If it answers "what was it like / what was happening", it's imparfait.
Correct my French: "Je suis 25 ans et je suis faim."

Corrected: « J'ai 25 ans et j'ai faim. »

French uses « avoir » (to have) where English uses "to be" for a whole family of states: age (« j'ai 25 ans »), hunger (« j'ai faim »), thirst (« j'ai soif »), being hot or cold (« j'ai chaud »), being right (« j'ai raison ») and being sleepy (« j'ai sommeil »). The logic is that these are things you possess temporarily, not what you are. Only « je suis fatigué » (tired) breaks the pattern — that one really does take « être ».
What does "avoir le cafard" mean? Something about a cockroach?

Literally "to have the cockroach" — it means to feel down, blue, melancholic. « Depuis son départ, il a le cafard » — since she left, he's been feeling low.

Baudelaire is credited with popularizing it in the 19th century; the cockroach stands for the dark, scuttling mood you can't shake. English's nearest equivalents are "to have the blues" or "to be down in the dumps" — the animal differs, the gloom is the same. For a temporary bad mood it's perfect; for anything more serious, French would say « être déprimé ».
Translate into English: «Il a beau essayer, il n'arrive jamais à arriver à l'heure.»

"No matter how hard he tries, he never manages to be on time."

The jewel here is « il a beau essayer » — « avoir beau » + infinitive means "to do something in vain / no matter how much..." The word « beau » (beautiful) is a red herring; nothing is pretty about it. The construction is always concessive: « Tu as beau crier, personne ne t'entend » — shout all you want, nobody hears you.
Why is "les enfants" pronounced like "lez-enfants"? When do I link words like that?

That's a liaison — a normally silent final consonant wakes up and attaches to the next word when it begins with a vowel. « Les‿enfants »: the s of « les » becomes a [z] sound bridging into « enfants ».

Some liaisons are obligatory: after articles and pronouns (« nous‿avons », « les‿amis », « vous‿êtes »). Some are forbidden: after « et », and before words starting with an aspirate h (« les héros », no link). And some are optional and make you sound more formal the more you use them. Rule of thumb for learners: always make them after « les, des, nous, vous, ils, elles » and numbers — skipping those is the one error every French ear notices.
Bonjour, je suis là pour l'entretien de dix heures avec Madame Fabre.
Bonjour, bienvenue. Vous êtes en avance, c'est parfait. Madame Fabre termine une réunion et sera à vous dans cinq minutes. Puis-je vous offrir un café en attendant ?
Volontiers, merci. C'est gentil.
Je vous en prie. Installez-vous dans la salle à côté. Au fait, vous avez apporté votre CV et la lettre de recommandation ? Madame Fabre aime les avoir sous les yeux pendant l'entretien.
How do I close a formal French letter? In English I'd write "Yours sincerely" before signing a job application cover letter.

The classic closing: « Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées. »

Yes, it's a whole sentence, and yes, it's expected — a bare « cordialement » on a first application can read as too light (save « cordialement » or « bien à vous » for established correspondence). The formula literally asks the reader to "accept the expression of my distinguished greetings." French administrative politeness is a ritual: the longer the formula, the more formal the intent. Match « Madame » / « Monsieur » to how you opened the letter.
Pourquoi dit-on « il faut que tu viennes » et pas « il faut que tu viens » ?

Parce qu'après « il faut que », le verbe passe au subjonctif : « que tu viennes », pas « que tu viens ».

La logique : l'indicatif présente les faits ; le subjonctif présente ce qui n'est pas encore un fait — obligations, désirs, doutes. « Il faut que » impose une nécessité, donc la venue n'est pas réelle au moment où l'on parle. Même famille : « je veux que tu viennes », « il est important qu'elle soit là », « bien qu'il pleuve ».

Pour les verbes réguliers en -er, le subjonctif ressemble au présent (« que tu parles »), c'est pourquoi l'erreur se cache. C'est avec « être », « avoir », « venir », « pouvoir » qu'elle devient visible.
Correct this: "Les fleurs que j'ai acheté sont sur la table."

One letter missing: « Les fleurs que j'ai achetées sont sur la table. »

In the passé composé with « avoir », the past participle normally never changes — except when the direct object comes BEFORE the verb. Here « que » stands for « les fleurs » (feminine plural) and sits in front of « acheté », so the participle must agree: achetées.

Compare: « J'ai acheté les fleurs » — object after the verb, no agreement, no -s. The rule only wakes up when the object jumps the queue, which is why « que » sentences are where it always hides.
My date never showed up and my French friend said "il t'a posé un lapin." A rabbit??

He stood you up. « Poser un lapin à quelqu'un » — literally "to place a rabbit on someone" — means to not show up for a meeting or date without warning.

The origin is murky (19th-century slang, possibly about unpaid debts and empty promises), but the usage is crystal clear and very common: « On avait rendez-vous à vingt heures, et il m'a posé un lapin. » If you want to complain about it the next day, add: « La prochaine fois, préviens-moi » — next time, let me know.
Bonjour, je cherche quelque chose contre le mal de tête, s'il vous plaît.
Bonjour. Vous avez de la fièvre aussi, ou seulement la douleur ? Et c'est pour vous ou pour un enfant ?
C'est pour moi, et non, pas de fièvre. Juste une grosse migraine depuis ce matin.

Alors je vous conseille du paracétamol, un gramme toutes les six heures, maximum trois par jour. Buvez beaucoup d'eau et reposez-vous dans le noir si vous pouvez. Si ça dure plus de deux jours, il faudra voir un médecin.
Translate: « Il pleut des cordes, on ferait mieux de rester à la maison. »

"It's raining ropes — we'd be better off staying home."

But no English speaker says "raining ropes"; the natural equivalent is "It's pouring" or the equally strange "It's raining cats and dogs." Both languages describe heavy rain with absurd falling objects — French chose ropes, English chose animals. A good translation keeps the meaning and swaps the image: « Il pleut des cordes » = "It's bucketing down."
At my French office everyone says "tu" to the boss. I thought "vous" was mandatory at work?

It depends entirely on the company's culture, and startups and creative industries have largely gone « tu » — even with the director. Traditional sectors (banking, law, administration) still run on « vous ».

The safe protocol as the newcomer: start with « vous », mirror what others use with YOU, and wait to be invited: « On peut se tutoyer ? » is a normal, friendly offer. Nobody is offended by an early « vous »; an early « tu » in a formal house can genuinely jar. Note the verbs: tutoyer (to say tu) and vouvoyer (to say vous) — French has single words for the whole negotiation.
How do you say "The train station is only a ten-minute walk from here" in German?

«Der Bahnhof ist von hier nur zehn Minuten zu Fuß entfernt.»

Worth stealing for your toolbox: «zu Fuß» (on foot, literally "by foot") and the «von hier ... entfernt» frame for distances. German often puts the whole journey description at the end, so the sentence lands on «entfernt» — "removed/away" — which acts like a second half of the verb "to be ... away".
Guten Tag! Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee und ein Stück Kuchen.
Guten Tag! Sehr gern. Wir haben heute Apfelkuchen und Käsekuchen. Was darf es sein?
Den Apfelkuchen, bitte. Und der Kaffee mit Milch.
Kommt sofort. Ein Apfelkuchen und ein Kaffee mit Milch. Möchten Sie sonst noch etwas — vielleicht ein Glas Wasser dazu?
When is it "auf dem Tisch" and when "auf den Tisch"? Both are translated as "on the table"!

German answers a question English doesn't ask: WHERE (location, no movement) takes the dative; WHERE TO (movement toward) takes the accusative.

- «Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch» — the book is lying on the table (where? dative: dem).
- «Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch» — I'm putting the book onto the table (where to? accusative: den).

Nine prepositions do this double duty (an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen) — the Wechselpräpositionen. Memory hook: dative = a photograph, accusative = a film clip. If something is in motion toward a goal, the camera is rolling.
Correct my German: "Ich habe gestern bin ins Kino gegangen."

Corrected: «Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen.»

You used two auxiliaries where German wants exactly one. «Gehen» forms its past with «sein», not «haben», because it expresses movement from A to B: «ich bin gegangen», «sie ist gefahren», «wir sind gelaufen». Verbs of movement and change of state take «sein»; nearly everything else takes «haben» («ich habe gegessen»). So delete «habe» and your sentence is perfect — word order and all.
My German colleague told me I have "Tomaten auf den Augen" — tomatoes on my eyes? I wasn't even eating.

He was teasing you: «Tomaten auf den Augen haben» means you're not seeing something that's right in front of you — the classic case is asking for your glasses while they're on your head.

«Du hast wohl Tomaten auf den Augen — der Schlüssel liegt doch direkt vor dir!» (The key is right in front of you!) English equivalents: "to be blind as a bat" or simply "open your eyes!" German loves food-based idioms for everyday blindness and confusion — compare «ein Brett vor dem Kopf haben», to have a plank in front of your head, when something obvious just won't click.
Translate into English: «Obwohl er den ganzen Tag gearbeitet hatte, half er uns noch beim Umzug.»

"Even though he had worked all day, he still helped us with the move."

Two things to notice. «Obwohl» sends its verb to the very end («gearbeitet hatte»), which is why the German reads backwards to English eyes. And «der Umzug» is specifically a house/apartment move — the relocation kind with boxes and furniture — not movement in general. German also needs «noch» here ("still/yet") to carry the sense of him helping despite everything; drop it and the sentence loses its little note of admiration.
Why does the verb jump to the end in "..., weil ich morgen arbeiten muss"?

Because «weil» is a subordinating conjunction: it opens a dependent clause, and in German dependent clauses the verb machinery moves to the end. «Ich muss morgen arbeiten» (main clause, verb second) becomes «..., weil ich morgen arbeiten muss» — «arbeiten muss» parked at the finish line.

Same behavior with «dass», «wenn», «obwohl», «als»: «Ich weiß, dass er heute keine Zeit hat.»

One spoken shortcut you'll hear constantly: people using «weil» with main-clause order («weil ich muss morgen arbeiten») — common in speech, marked as sloppy in writing. Learn the verb-final form first; it's never wrong.
Entschuldigung, ich suche den Zug nach München. Von welchem Gleis fährt er ab?
Der Zug nach München fährt heute von Gleis sieben ab, in etwa zwanzig Minuten. Es gibt aber eine kleine Verspätung, also eher um halb drei.
Danke. Und wo kann ich meine Fahrkarte kaufen?
Die Automaten stehen gleich dort drüben, neben dem Kiosk. Sie können auch mit Karte zahlen. Eine gute Reise wünsche ich Ihnen!
Correct this: "Mir geht es gut, danke. Und dich?"

Just the last word: «Mir geht es gut, danke. Und dir?»

«Wie geht es...?» pairs with the dative, because the formula is really "how does it go FOR you" — the person is the experiencer, not the doer. So: «Mir geht es gut», «Wie geht es dir?», formal «Wie geht es Ihnen?» Your instinct with «dich» (accusative) is understandable, but the fixed phrase never uses it. The short answer to «Und dir?» is simply «Auch gut, danke!»
What is "Feierabend"? My German coworkers treat it almost like a holiday every single day.

Feierabend is the part of the day after work ends — but it's more than a time of day; it's a protected institution. The word originally meant the evening before a feast day, and it still carries that whiff of sacredness: when Germans say «Jetzt ist Feierabend», work is OVER, fully, and email can wait until tomorrow.

You'll also hear it as a full stop in conversation: «So, Feierabend!» — that's it, we're done here. Trying to schedule a meeting "nach Feierabend" is fine socially, but asking someone to keep working through it, casually, marks you as not yet understanding the culture.
Translate into German, formal register: "Thank you for your quick reply. I would like to confirm our appointment on Thursday at 3 p.m."

«Vielen Dank für Ihre schnelle Antwort. Ich möchte unseren Termin am Donnerstag um 15 Uhr bestätigen.»

Formal choices to note: «Ihre» with a capital I (the possessive of «Sie»), «möchte» rather than «will» for a courteous "would like", and the 24-hour clock — «15 Uhr» is standard in written German; «drei Uhr nachmittags» would sound translated. If the appointment was the other party's suggestion, «bestätigen» can soften to «gerne bestätigen» — gladly confirm.
German adjective endings are a nightmare. Is there a survivable strategy?

Yes: learn the signal, not the table. The adjective's job is to repeat gender/case information — but only when the article hasn't already done it.

1. After «der/die/das» (the article already shouts the gender), the adjective relaxes to -e or -en: «der kleine Hund», «die kleine Katze», «dem kleinen Hund».
2. After «ein» words, the adjective must carry the signal itself in nominative: «ein kleiner Hund», «eine kleine Katze», «ein kleines Kind».
3. With no article at all, the adjective does all the work: «kaltes Wasser», «frische Milch».

And one mercy rule: in the plural with «die», it's almost always -en («die kleinen Hunde», «mit den kleinen Hunden»). Master these three scenes and you cover the vast majority of real sentences; the full table is sixteen cells of mostly -en.
How do you say "I've lived in Shanghai for three years, but my Chinese is still not very good" in Mandarin?

«我在上海住了三年了，可是我的中文还是不太好。」(Wǒ zài Shànghǎi zhù le sān nián le, kěshì wǒ de Zhōngwén hái shì bú tài hǎo.)

Notice the double 了: the first marks the completed action (lived), the second — at the end — marks "up to now and still continuing", which is exactly the meaning of "for three years (so far)". And «还是不太好» softens the self-criticism: 还是 (still, as before) + 不太好 (not too good). It's a humble, natural sentence — Chinese listeners will appreciate the modesty built into it.
服务员，我想点菜。你们这里有什么招牌菜？
欢迎光临！我们的招牌菜是红烧肉和清蒸鱼，都是师傅的拿手菜。您几位用餐？
两位。就来一个红烧肉、一个清蒸鱼，再加一个青菜。
好的。一份红烧肉、一份清蒸鱼、一个炒青菜。请问要米饭吗？茶水马上给您倒上。
Why can't I just use 个 for everything? 一条鱼, 一张纸, 一本书 — what are all these words doing?

Those are measure words (量词), and Chinese requires one between a number and a noun — think of English "two LOAVES of bread" or "three SHEETS of paper", except Chinese does it for every noun.

The good news: 个 is the universal backup and nobody will misunderstand «一个鱼». The better news: the common ones follow shapes. 条 is for long, thin, flexible things — 一条鱼 (fish), 一条河 (river), 一条裤子 (trousers). 张 is for flat surfaces — 一张纸 (paper), 一张桌子 (table), 一张票 (ticket). 本 is for bound volumes — 一本书, 一本杂志. Learn 个 plus these five — 条, 张, 本, 只 (animals), 杯 (cups of) — and you'll sound right 90% of the time.
Correct my Chinese: 我昨天没去了商店，所以没买牛奶。

Corrected: 我昨天没去商店，所以没买牛奶。(Wǒ zuótiān méi qù shāngdiàn, suǒyǐ méi mǎi niúnǎi.)

The problem is the 了 in 没去了. 了 marks something as completed — but 没 says it did NOT happen. They contradict each other: you can't mark a non-event as completed. The rule is absolute and mercifully simple: wherever 没(有) negates a verb, 了 must disappear. Compare the positive twin: 我昨天去了商店 — yesterday I DID go to the store, and there 了 is welcome.
My Chinese teacher described my homework as 马马虎虎. Was that good or bad?

Neither praise nor disaster — it means "so-so, passable, just okay". Literally 马马虎虎 is "horse horse tiger tiger", and the old story goes that a careless painter drew a creature that was half horse, half tiger — neither one properly. That's the flavor: careless, half-done, good enough to pass.

You'll hear it most as a modest answer to 你最近怎么样？(How have you been?) — 马马虎虎，还行 (so-so, getting by). From a teacher it's a gentle push: acceptable, but you can do better. It was not a compliment, but it was friendly.
Translate into English: «这件事不能急，我们得一步一步来，慢慢商量出一个大家都满意的办法。」

"This matter can't be rushed; we need to take it step by step and slowly work out a solution that everyone is satisfied with."

«一步一步来» is one of those phrases Chinese reaches for constantly — literally "come one step, one step" — and it carries a calming, procedural tone: proceed methodically. «商量出» is also worth noticing: 商量 (discuss) plus the result complement 出 (out), meaning the discussion must PRODUCE something — a 办法 (way/plan) everyone can accept. English "talk it out" is the closest cousin.
我来介绍一下，这是我妈妈，这是我弟弟。他今年上大学了。
阿姨好！弟弟好！我常听她提起你们。弟弟在大学学什么专业？
他学计算机，平时喜欢打篮球。
计算机好啊，现在很热门。弟弟个子这么高，打篮球肯定很厉害。大家快请坐，我去给你们倒茶。
了 and 过 both seem to mean past. 我去了北京 vs 我去过北京 — what's the real difference?

They answer different questions. 了 reports that an action was completed: 我去了北京 = "I went to Beijing" (on some occasion we're talking about — maybe last week, maybe I'm still there). 过 marks EXPERIENCE — "have ever done it at some point in life": 我去过北京 = "I have been to Beijing (before)".

Tests: with 过 you can add frequency — 我去过三次北京 (I've been three times). And the negatives split cleanly: 没去 = didn't go (that time); 没去过 = have never been. If a Chinese speaker asks 你去过长城吗？, they're asking about your life experience, not your last trip — answer with 去过 or 没去过, never with 了.
What does the chengyu 画蛇添足 mean? My textbook lists it without a story.

画蛇添足 (huà shé tiān zú) — "draw a snake and add feet": to ruin something by adding unnecessary extras. The story: in ancient Chu, several men competed to draw a snake fastest, the prize being a pot of wine. The winner finished early, and with time to spare he smugly added feet to his snake — at which point another man snatched the wine, saying: a snake has no feet; yours is no longer a snake.

It's the perfect criticism of over-engineering: the report was finished, but you 画蛇添足'd it with three extra charts. English's closest: "to gild the lily."
How do I say "The earlier we leave, the less traffic there will be" in Chinese?

«我们越早出发，路上的车就越少。」(Wǒmen yuè zǎo chūfā, lùshang de chē jiù yuè shǎo.)

Chinese handles "the more... the more..." with a doubled 越: 越 + adjective/verb, then 越 again in the second half — 我们越早出发 (the earlier we set out), 车就越少 (the fewer cars there will be, with 就 linking the result). The pattern is a frame you can refill endlessly: 越快越好 (the faster the better), 你越说我越糊涂 (the more you explain, the more confused I get). No comparative endings, no word order gymnastics — just 越...越.
How do I politely say "Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the station?" in Japanese?

「すみません、駅へはどう行けばいいですか。」(Sumimasen, eki e wa dō ikeba ii desu ka.)

Breakdown of the politeness: すみません opens softly (excuse me / sorry to bother you). どう行けばいいですか is literally "how should I go?" — the ば conditional doing the work of "could you tell me". A shorter, equally polite version: 「すみません、駅はどこですか。」(Where is the station?) For strangers, always use the です/ます style as here; plain form would sound like you're talking to a close friend.
すみません、この近くにコンビニはありますか。
はい、ありますよ。この道をまっすぐ行って、二つ目の信号を右に曲がると、左側にあります。歩いて三分くらいです。
ありがとうございます。夜遅くまで開いていますか。
はい、あのコンビニは二十四時間営業です。夜中でも大丈夫ですよ。
は vs が — both translate as nothing in English and I never know which one to use. Help.

The shortest useful rule: は marks the TOPIC (what we're talking about), が marks the SUBJECT in focus (who/what is doing or being something, often new information).

「私は学生です」— as for me (topic), I'm a student. 「私が学生です」— I'M the one who is a student (answering "who here is a student?").

Classic contrast: 「象は鼻が長い」— the elephant (は, topic): its nose (が) is long. New information and question words take が: 「誰が来ましたか」(who came?) and the answer mirrors it: 「田中さんが来ました」. When in doubt in simple statements, は is the safer default; が is for introducing, emphasizing, and answering who/what questions.
Correct my Japanese: 私は昨日、映画を見ます。とても面白かったです。

One tense mismatch: 私は昨日、映画を見ました。とても面白かったです。

Your second sentence is already in the past (面白かった, "was interesting"), so the first must be too: 見ます (watch/will watch) becomes 見ました (watched). Japanese is strict about this chain — once 昨日 (yesterday) sets the time frame, every verb in the story lives there. Your word order and particles were all correct; this was purely a tense agreement slip.
What does 猿も木から落ちる mean? Even monkeys fall from trees?

Exactly that — and the meaning is the comfort inside the image: even experts make mistakes. A monkey is the master of trees; if even a monkey sometimes falls, your error is no disgrace.

Usage: a veteran chef burns a dish, a champion misspells a simple word — 猿も木から落ちる (saru mo ki kara ochiru). It's said with sympathy, usually to console someone senior who slipped, never to mock. The closest English cousins are "to err is human" and "even Homer sometimes nods." Japanese proverb style (kotowaza) loves this move: one concrete animal picture carrying a whole philosophy of fallibility.
Translate into English: 「来週の会議は三時からですが、資料は前日までにメールで送ってください。」

"Next week's meeting starts at three, but please send the materials by email by the day before."

Two business-Japanese staples: 前日 (zenjitsu, the day before — a deadline word you'll see constantly) and までに (made ni, "by" a deadline — contrast with まで, "until", which describes duration: 三時まで働く, work until three). And 送ってください is the standard polite request form; in a real office email it might upgrade to 送っていただけますか, but ください is never wrong.
How do I turn verbs into requests? I know 待ってください means "please wait" but I can't build my own.

You need the て-form (te-form), then add ください. The て-form patterns by verb group:

- る-verbs (食べる, 見る): drop る, add て → 食べて, 見て.
- う-verbs: the last sound shifts to the て row — 書く→書いて, 話す→話して, 読む→読んで, 買う→買って.
- Irregulars, just memorize: する→して, 来る→来て.

Then: 食べてください (please eat), 書いてください (please write), 読んでください (please read). One famous exception to the sound rules: 行く (to go) becomes 行って, not 行きて — every learner trips on it exactly once. The て-form also chains actions (起きて、顔を洗って...), so this one pattern unlocks half the language.
はじめまして。本日からお世話になります、田中と申します。よろしくお願いいたします。
はじめまして、田中さん。こちらこそ、よろしくお願いいたします。私は営業部の佐藤です。何か分からないことがあれば、遠慮なく聞いてくださいね。
ありがとうございます。頑張りますので、ご指導よろしくお願いいたします。
頼もしいですね。まずは今日の午後、チームの皆さんに紹介します。一緒に頑張りましょう。
How do you say "My name is Daniel, I'm from Canada, and I'm learning Hindi because I love Indian films" in Hindi?

«मेरा नाम डैनियल है, मैं कनाडा से हूँ, और मैं हिंदी सीख रहा हूँ क्योंकि मुझे भारतीय फ़िल्में बहुत पसंद हैं।» (Merā nām Ḍainiyal hai, main Kanāḍā se hū̃, aur main Hindī sīkh rahā hū̃ kyōṅki mujhe Bhāratīya filmẽ bahut pasand haĩ.)

Structures worth copying: «मैं ... से हूँ» for origin, «सीख रहा हूँ» (am learning — the रहा progressive), and «मुझे ... पसंद हैं» for liking, where the thing liked controls the verb, so plural फ़िल्में takes हैं. One sentence, four load-bearing patterns.
भैया, ये आम कितने के हैं?
ये वाले सौ रुपये किलो हैं, और ये छोटे वाले अस्सी के। बिल्कुल मीठे हैं, खाकर देखिए।
सौ तो ज़्यादा है। सत्तर में दो किलो दे दो।
चलो, आपके लिए पचहत्तर लगा देता हूँ। दो किलो तौल दूँ? केले भी ताज़े आए हैं आज।
Hindi word order confuses me. "I gave the book to Ravi" — where does everything go?

Hindi is verb-final: Subject – Object – Verb, and the little relation words (postpositions) come AFTER the noun, not before. So: «मैंने रवि को किताब दी।» — literally "I (मैंने) to-Ravi (रवि को) book (किताब) gave (दी)".

Three things to notice. को follows रवि (postposition, like a preposition flipped). The perfective subject takes ने (मैंने, not मैं) — a famous Hindi quirk with transitive verbs in the past. And the verb दी agrees with किताब (feminine), not with you. Build the sentence backwards from the verb and the rest falls into place.
Correct my Hindi: मैं कल दिल्ली जाता था और वहाँ मेरे दोस्त से मिला।

Corrected: मैं कल दिल्ली गया और वहाँ अपने दोस्त से मिला। (Main kal Dillī gayā aur vahā̃ apne dost se milā.)

The issue is जाता था — that's the habitual past, "I used to go", for repeated actions in the past. But कल (yesterday) names one single trip, so Hindi wants the simple perfective गया (went). Rule of thumb: a specific day or a counted event → गया/आया/खाया forms; a routine or "back in those days" → जाता था/खाता था forms. Your से मिला (met with) was already right — मिलना takes से, not को.
Someone at work said "दाल में कुछ काला है" about a suspicious deal. Something black in the lentils?

It means "something fishy is going on" — literally "there's something black in the dal". The image is homely and perfect: you're eating your lentils, you spot something dark that shouldn't be there, and you know the whole dish is suspect.

Usage: prices that change every time you ask, a contract with one clause nobody will explain — दाल में कुछ काला है. The fuller version adds ज़रूर (certainly): दाल में ज़रूर कुछ काला है. English's "something smells off" is the nearest cousin; Hindi just locates the suspicion in the kitchen, where all important intelligence is gathered.
Translate into English: «मेहनत का फल हमेशा मीठा होता है, इसलिए हार मत मानो, बस कोशिश करते रहो।»

"The fruit of hard work is always sweet, so don't give up — just keep trying."

मेहनत का फल (the fruit of effort) is a set phrase, and मीठा (sweet) does the same work as English "sweet success". हार मत मानो is literally "don't accept defeat" — मानना is to accept/acknowledge, so giving up is framed as agreeing to lose. And करते रहो (keep doing) uses रहना as an auxiliary of continuation: verb stem + ते रहो = keep on doing it. Warm, proverb-flavored encouragement — the kind of sentence Indian grandparents deploy with precision.
How do you say "Thank you very much for your help; I really appreciate it" in Arabic?

«شكرًا جزيلًا على مساعدتك، أنا أقدّر ذلك حقًّا.» (Shukran jazīlan ʿalā musāʿadatik, anā uqaddiru dhālika ḥaqqan.)

شكرًا جزيلًا is the strong form of thanks — جزيلًا means "abundantly", so it's warmer than plain شكرًا. To a woman, the ending changes: مساعدتكِ (musāʿadatiki). Arabic also loves to escalate gratitude with a blessing in return — بارك الله فيك (may God bless you) — which in everyday life functions as a heartfelt thank-you all by itself.
السلام عليكم! اسمي سارة، أنا من لبنان. تشرفنا!
وعليكم السلام، أهلًا وسهلًا بك يا سارة! أنا عمر، من مصر. فرصة سعيدة جدًّا. ماذا تعملين؟
أنا معلّمة لغة عربية. وأنت؟
أنا مهندس، وأحبّ تعليم اللغات أيضًا. أهلًا بك في أيّ وقت، بيتنا بيتك.
My course teaches Modern Standard Arabic but Egyptians in films say completely different words. Am I learning the wrong Arabic?

No — you're learning the trunk; the dialects are the branches. Modern Standard Arabic (الفصحى, al-Fuṣḥā) is the language of news, books, official documents and formal speech across all 22 Arab countries; every educated speaker understands it. But daily life runs on dialects (العامية), and Egyptian is the most widely understood of them because Egypt's film and TV industry dominated the region for a century.

Concrete example: "how are you?" is كيف حالك؟ in MSA, but ازّيك؟ (izzayyak) in Cairo and شلونك؟ in the Gulf/Iraq. Strategy: master MSA first for reading and being understood everywhere, then add one dialect for conversation — Egyptian for maximum reach, Levantine for a close second.
Correct my Arabic: السيارة جديد وأنا اشتريتها أمس.

One small fix: السيارة جديدة وأنا اشتريتها أمس. (As-sayyāra jadīda wa-anā ishtaraytuhā ams.)

The adjective must match the noun's gender: السيارة (car) is feminine — you can tell by the ة (tā' marbūṭa) at its end — so "new" must be جديدة with the feminine ending, not جديد. This agreement runs everywhere: كتاب جديد (a new book, masculine) but سيارة جديدة, مكتبة كبيرة (a big library). Your اشتريتها أمس (I bought it yesterday) was flawless — object pronoun attached exactly right.
What does the proverb الصبر مفتاح الفرج mean, and when do people say it?

الصبر مفتاح الفرج (aṣ-ṣabr miftāḥ al-faraj) — "Patience is the key to relief/deliverance." Not just "good things take time": فرج specifically means the release that comes after hardship, the knot finally loosening.

People say it to comfort someone in a genuinely hard stretch — waiting for exam results, a visa, a sick relative to recover. It's one of the most quoted sayings in the Arab world, half proverb, half prayer. A close relative you'll also hear: إنّ مع العسر يسرًا — "with hardship comes ease" — quoted from the Quran and used the same way, as a hand on the shoulder in sentence form.
How do you say "We had a wonderful time in Florence; the food was incredible and the people were so kind" in Italian?

«Ci siamo divertiti moltissimo a Firenze; il cibo era incredibile e la gente era gentilissima.»

Two very Italian choices here. "To have a wonderful time" is reflexive: «divertirsi» — literally "we amused ourselves greatly", and in the past it needs «essere»: ci siamo divertiti (with moltissimo doing the work of "wonderful"). And for "so kind", Italian reaches for the absolute superlative gentilissima — just add -issimo to the adjective, no "very" needed. One more: Firenze, not "Florence" — city names get translated too.
Buongiorno! Vorrei un cono piccolo, per favore. Che gusti avete?
Buongiorno! Abbiamo stracciatella, pistacchio, nocciola, limone e il classico fiordilatte. Vuole assaggiare il pistacchio? È il nostro migliore.
Sì, grazie... È buonissimo! Allora pistacchio e stracciatella.
Perfetto, un cono piccolo con pistacchio e stracciatella. Sono tre euro e cinquanta. Buona giornata e buona passeggiata!
Correct my Italian: "Penso che è vero, ma spero che lui viene domani."

Both verbs after «che» need the subjunctive: «Penso che sia vero, ma spero che lui venga domani.»

«Pensare che» and «sperare che» express opinions and hopes — not facts — so Italian switches the following verb into the subjunctive: è → sia, viene → venga. The indicative is reserved for certainty: «So che è vero» (I KNOW it's true) keeps «è». A memory hook: the stronger your claim to knowledge, the calmer the verb. Doubt, hope, opinion, emotion — subjunctive territory, every time.
Before my exam an Italian friend said "in bocca al lupo!" — into the wolf's mouth?? And I was supposed to answer something?

It's the Italian "break a leg!" — literally "into the mouth of the wolf". Hunters once wished each other the most dangerous place imaginable, as a charm against bad luck.

And yes, there's a required reply: «Crepi!» — short for «Crepi il lupo», "may the wolf die!" Never answer «grazie» — traditionally that breaks the spell and brings the bad luck back. Modern speakers are relaxing about it, but in an exam hall, «crepi» is the answer that earns the smile. Use «in bocca al lupo» before exams, performances, interviews — anywhere English would say "good luck" with feeling.
